1:
Calvin supplies the history the opening verse assumes. Jeconiah reigned three months before surrendering of his own accord to the army of the king of Babylon, and since so short a reign was reckoned as nothing, the word that Jehoiakim should have no legitimate successor stood fulfilled. Nebuchadnezzar, seeing the people could hardly be kept in order without a king, made Mattaniah king and renamed him Zedekiah, as Gill records. Calvin adds the motive for the revolt that followed: no new provocation had occurred, and the king wanted only to be free of tribute and of the reproach of reigning by another leave. Ellicott notes that the eight chapters beginning here form a continuous narrative of the later fortunes of the prophet, and that the deposed king name appears shortened; Calvin takes the curtailment as deliberate, a clipping by way of reproach.

Ellicott reads the second verse as a general survey of the reign, placed before a history that falls near its close; and he distinguishes the groups named, the servants being the king personal attendants rather than the princes of Judah. Calvin insists the disobedience runs wider than politics: Zedekiah was condemned not only for breaking faith with the king who set him up but for keeping his fathers superstitions and refusing to be called back to the law, and the fate of the previous king stood before their eyes without sobering them. Gill records a contrary reading from Jarchi, that Jehoiakim was wicked while his people were righteous and Zedekiah righteous while his people were wicked; but he thinks it rests on the single act of taking the prophet out of prison, whereas king and people alike were corrupt.

Henry sets the same point as a rebuke: those have hearts wretchedly hard who watch judgments fall on others, feel them on themselves, and still will not be humbled.

The request for prayer is where Henry is sharpest, and he refuses to make it simply hypocrisy: it shows some sense of the king need and some esteem for good men. Yet it condemns him out of his own mouth, since he wanted the prophet good prayers and would not take his good counsel, and it is common for those to desire to be prayed for who will not be advised. The king would have done better to send for the prophet to pray with him than to send to him to pray for him, but he thought that beneath him, and no one can expect the comforts of religion who will not stoop to its services.

Clarke reads it the same way: the king would hear a message from the Lord provided it agreed with his own mind, and did not fully trust his own prophets. Ellicott supplies the occasion and suspects the errand. The besiegers had withdrawn on hearing of the advance of Pharaoh-Hophra, whom he identifies with the Apries of Herodotus, and the king seems to have judged the moment right for asserting independence. The two men sent belonged to the party opposed to submission and were hostile to him, one appearing later as his accuser; so their errand was either bare official obedience or an attempt to win him by a show of religious zeal, and Ellicott thinks the stress they lay on praying to the Lord our God makes the second likelier. Calvin describes the state of mind behind it: the king was elated by the prospect of Egyptian help and anxious at once, as the ungodly must be, tossed about while trying to confirm themselves in security. Such men seek God, he says, but not in earnest, discharging the outward duty while bringing neither faith nor repentance, by which alone access to him is opened. Gill notes a small question about the messengers, whether the priestly title belongs to the second alone, as the accents indicate, or to both, as the Syriac reads it.
4:
The note that the prophet was at liberty is read for what it implies. Gill contrasts the previous reign, when he and Baruch had to hide from men sent to take them. Calvin allows that he may have been in prison earlier and released when the rage cooled. Ellicott makes the sharpest use of it: the remark is made with the later imprisonment in view, since the prophet was free when the message reached him, and it was his answer to that message that put him in prison.

The Egyptian advance is filled in from history. Gill recalls that Zedekiah had sworn homage to the king of Babylon, then rebelled and made a league with Egypt, whose king, though he came no more in person after his defeat at Carchemish, did send his army. Clarke, who ties the prophet liberty to the raising of the siege and marks it temporary, names the Egyptian Pharaoh-hophra or Apries, reigning in place of his father Necho, and has Nebuchadnezzar raise the siege suddenly to meet him, Zedekiah using the interval to ask whether they might now count themselves safe. Ellicott adds that the force was sent as the result of negotiations, and was strong in chariots and horses.

Calvin argues for a particular moment. He thinks it improbable the messengers went out when the report first spread, and likelier after the city was relieved, since everything still hung on an uncertain battle: an Egyptian victory promised peace, a defeat left the city helpless. Out of that suspense he draws his account of the king religion. Hypocrites are driven to seek the aid of a God they despise, not for show but because they are brought to straits in which they feel their need; they would strip him of authority if they could, but being forced to know that he reigns, necessity constrains them to pray formally.

Calvin notes that Zedekiah, too guilty to pray himself, put the prophet between himself and God; and grants that the faithful do something that looks the same, since they too ask others to join them. The difference is that the godly are not content with their own prayers and still pray, while the hypocrite, thinking access forbidden and himself unworthy, substitutes another and does not pray at all, wishing the whole world to pray for him and never seeking for himself.

Keil and Delitzsch head the following section as the imprisonment of the prophet, set in the interval when the besiegers had withdrawn. The answer itself is grim. Clarke says the Egyptians were defeated and, not being hearty in the cause, returned at once, leaving the besieger free to resume; Calvin leaves the cause open, whether they were beaten or merely struck with fear and retired to secure their own cities. Ellicott points to the same prediction elsewhere, connected there with the appeal to Egypt being a plain breach of compact, and observes that this relief, like an earlier one in the Assyrian invasion, brought only a temporary suspension and ended in the conquest of Egypt.

Calvin catches something the narrative has not said. The messengers were sent to ask prayer, but the answer speaks of the king sending to inquire, so he wanted a favourable oracle as well, Scripture often mentioning only one of two things included. He presses it with a question: why apply to this man rather than the chief priest, unless the king knew him to be a true prophet? The reply reproves him indirectly, since he sent as though ready to hear whatever God might say and was not. Hypocrites who take a circuitous route do not get what they want, because they try to transform God into their own character rather than bend themselves to his word. Gill adds that the titles in the reply are the usual ones taken when God spoke by this prophet.
9:
Gill takes the warning against self-deception at the word: the phrase may be rendered deceive not your souls, or lift not up your souls with vain hopes; and he calls self-deception a dreadful thing, the disappointment being bitterest when a man has been elated by a hope that was never real. Calvin explains why the warning had to be added. Zedekiah might have been shaken by the first answer and grown harder under it, as hypocrites do, who on finding they can gain nothing become furious against God and run headlong on; so the prophet blocks the retreat before the king can take it.

The next verse is the strongest sentence in the chapter, and every voice reads it as a statement about who is really doing the work. Clarke calls the words strong and takes them as showing how fully God was determined to give the city up to fire and sword. Wesley puts the principle in two lines: when God is resolved upon an effect the instruments are little to be regarded, since what is in question is not the arm of flesh but the power of God. Calvin builds it out. The Jews were forming their judgment from fortunate events, and he infers from the necessity of the warning that they had repelled some attacks successfully and were nursing hopes on the strength of it. Against that he sets the principle that the ruin was never to be effected by the number of the besieging army or the valour of its soldiers but by the judgment of God, who could destroy them with a breath though no enemy existed at all.

Calvin presses the detail the verse leaves out. It says nothing of assault or capture, only of a burning; and wounded men rising each from his tent, scattered and without order or banner, are not an army in any ordinary sense. No valour and no skill are needed to set fire to a city, a thing women and children have often done to whole towns; so it is enough that the Chaldeans are armed by God, and even half dead they are strong enough for the work. Gill takes the clause more plainly, as a supposition that the whole besieging force had been beaten by the Egyptian allies and only a remnant left.

At the withdrawal the narrative turns to the prophet himself, and Henry notes how much of that narrative there is. This prophet relates more passages concerning himself than any other, and Henry defends it, since the histories of the lives and sufferings of the ministers of God have served the church as much as their preaching. Gill marks the moment simply, that the siege was raised and the army gone.

Henry reads the attempt to leave as a settled decision rather than a flight. In the lull the people went out into the country to look after their affairs, and the prophet meant to slip away among them, following the marginal reading; and Henry finds the manner characteristic. Though a man of great eminence he could reconcile himself to obscurity, and though one of a thousand was content to be lost in the crowd and buried alive in a corner or a cottage. Whether he was making for his own town does not appear, and the neighbours there had given him reason enough not to go unless they had mended; he may have meant to hide where he was not known, and so have his old wish for a lodging place in the wilderness. What settles it for Henry is the ministry rather than the danger: the prophet found he could do no good in the city and had laboured there in vain, and there are times when it is the wisdom of good men to retire into privacy and shut the doors about them.
12:
Why the prophet left and what he meant to do there are separate questions. Gill leaves the motive open three ways: to avoid the prison he expected, to escape the destruction he was certain of, or because he could do no good by preaching. Ellicott settles on the first, that he feared his answer would move the king to anger and lead, as it did, to an order for his arrest, the raising of the siege giving him free egress. Calvin makes the same point, since until then the gates were shut and the city ringed with enemies. Clarke judges that he withdrew from a city devoted to destruction in which he could do no more good.

On the errand the voices divide over one obscure clause. Ellicott renders it more accurately as taking a share from thence in the midst of the people, and takes that as the ostensible reason: a priest of Anathoth had property in Benjamin and went to look after it, whether to plough or to draw his share of the produce. If this was a sabbatical year he thinks the ploughing likelier, and the clause about the people is then explained, since it shows nothing clandestine in the journey. Other renderings proposed he calls less satisfactory. Clarke reports the same reading from Blayney, who supposed he went to collect the proceeds of a patrimony the besiegers had been sitting on, and notes the Chaldee agrees; against it he sets Dahler, that he went to withdraw himself from the siege as other inhabitants did.

Calvin refuses the property reading. The verb means to divide or scatter, so some give that he went to divide his heritage, which he calls harsh and forced; and the addition about the people, as though he meant to make his land common, has nothing probable in it. He prefers what most interpreters hold, that the prophet sought a quiet place and meant to be secluded among his own. Wesley keeps it simplest: knowing the city would soon be taken, the prophet set out for his own country in the crowd going out.

Keil and Delitzsch identify the gate as the north gate, through which the road ran to Benjamin and Ephraim, so that it is elsewhere called by the other name, and gloss the title of the officer as holder of the oversight. Ellicott adds that this officer was probably brother to one of the men sent earlier, and so likely to have known what answer was given. The charge is treated by everyone as a construction put on the prophet known position rather than on anything he did. Clarke says his enemies took occasion from his constant declaration that the city would fall to allege that he was in the besiegers interest. Ellicott sharpens it: the assumption was that though the army had gone he was making for its camp to urge it back and so fulfil his own prediction, and the very phrase used against him may allude to words he had himself spoken. Keil and Delitzsch grant the accusation was founded on his well-known views but call it mere sophistry, since the enemy were no longer lying before the city at all.

Calvin turns the episode into a reflection on reputation. The servants of God cannot escape calumny, and the danger here was to a name as well as a life, which to ingenuous men is worth more. He might have evaded the journey by pleading that he would offer his life a hundred times but gained nothing by being taken for a traitor, since the name of God would be exposed to blasphemy. Calvin allows the force of that, and says faithful teachers ought to remove every occasion of calumny as far as they can; but when they have done all they will not exempt themselves, their words and deeds being misconstrued anyway.
15:
The hearing before the princes was no hearing at all. Gill says they listened to the officer and would not hear him. Clarke says he was beaten without any proof of the alleged treachery and without form of justice. Calvin adds that he had his defence prepared and would only have been speaking to the deaf; and draws a rule from it, that self-government is necessary in an equitable judge, since where the mind is inflamed with wrath no rectitude can prevail. He also glosses the beating: it is hardly likely the princes struck him with their own fists, so they must have ordered servants to it, which is why some render that they caused him to be smitten.

Clarke explains that in eastern countries an officer of the law keeps an apartment in his house for confining the accused, and the scribe had one. Ellicott thinks the house was chosen because its owner exercised functions like a minister of police, and notes that besides the usual dungeon it had separate cells, the word for which occurs nowhere else. He measures the many days by the imprisonment beginning before a second siege of nearly two years, the prophet still in the court of the prison when the city fell.

Gill calls it the house of the pit, dark and dismal, Wesley a deep hole with cells in which they kept men judged great malefactors; Clarke makes the cells niches cut in the sides, citing Blayney. Calvin finds the versions uncertain. He cannot see why some render the word victualling houses; the best explanation makes them cells, the dungeon being a deep pit with niches scooped near the bottom so prisoners could lodge clear of the mire. His own emphasis falls on the narrowness: he was so cramped he could hardly sit or lie down or stand erect. It was cruel enough that an innocent man should be imprisoned after a beating, but a deep and dark place, and a space as good as fetters, was a great addition.

Keil and Delitzsch raise a construction point. Most interpreters attach the verse about the dungeon to what precedes, as a further account of the wrath of the princes; but the words do not properly allow it, since the sentence would be long and lumbering and the clause stands too far from the verb. They make it open a new section instead.

The enemy had returned, Gill notes, and the king was frightened. Calvin turns the summons into a character sketch, careful to be fair. Zedekiah was not among the worst, since he sent of his own accord and wished to find whether God could be appeased; he would not submit to the word, yet was not cruel enough to rage against the man. But this, Calvin says, is the usual way with hypocrites, who would be reconciled to God and remain free at once, wanting him to give place to them. He notes why the question was put privately, since asking openly would have cost the king his authority. Ellicott reads the same mixture: the king was at once better than his counsellors and afraid of them.

Calvin rejects one reading of the question, that the king asked whether the earlier prophecies had been true, holding that he wanted something new. The answer is where every voice stops to admire. Clarke calls it bold faithfulness, and to a king in whose hands the prophet life lay. Ellicott says not even the hope of protection moves him to change one jot of his message; he answers with a stern abruptness, adding the new prediction that the king himself will be taken. Calvin makes the courage costlier by remembering where the man had come from, a prison that had been to him like a grave; he feared both prison and death, and still presented his life as a sacrifice rather than soften his message.
18:
Ellicott hears in the protest something wrung out by the cruelty of the treatment, since the only crime chargeable was speaking the word given him, and no act of treachery could be proved. Calvin turns the question into a general one about the authority of rulers. Earthly princes are so proud, he says, that the moment they order anything they wish all dispute about their authority suspended, wanting their ordinances counted laws, when by following their own wills they often decree what is wholly unjust. Against that he sets the prophet flat denial of having sinned, though he had threatened the king and denounced ruin on city and temple; and beside it the other prophet who said he had not sinned against God or the king, having disregarded a royal decree rather than flatter a king into the place of God. Princes, he concludes, are not absolved before God merely because they will not bear their decrees disregarded, and a man may openly assert his innocence when it is not lawful to obey an impious edict.

The challenge to the rival prophets is put three ways. Clarke compares the predictions: they said the enemy would not come, he said they would, and they came. Ellicott adds that they had promised deliverance within two years and the city had been besieged instead, and that the withdrawal revived their credit, so they were now assuring the king the Egyptian army would make short work of the besiegers. Gill hears a challenge to appear and answer the charge of lying, and catches the contrast, the true prophet in prison while the false ones were caressed in the palaces.

The petition changes the register, and Gill marks it exactly: when the prophet spoke in the name of the Lord it was with boldness and majesty, and when he spoke for himself with the submission proper to a subject, owning as sovereign a prince whose destruction he knew was at hand. Clarke says he had been so ill used as to endanger his life; Ellicott, that half-starved in a foul dungeon he felt a return would be death. Calvin makes the request the point: the prophet dreaded death as other men do and yet governed himself so that fear never turned him aside, since the prophets were not logs of wood and had not iron hearts. He will not soften an honest profession of the truth to provide for his own safety.

The concession is read as providence working through a divided king. Gill notes that he did not discharge the prophet entirely, for fear of offending the princes, but moved him to a court of the prison where his friends could be admitted. Clarke adds that the court adjoined the royal house and the bread came from public stores; Ellicott infers from its being above ground that the king could see the prophet treated with respect. Calvin credits the change to a hidden working of the Spirit, and notes what the mercy did not extend to.

On the daily ration the two pull different ways. Ellicott is interested in the street, named nowhere else, and explains that the city seems to have assigned quarters to particular trades; he takes the order as evidence of a blockade. Calvin is interested in the bread. Some render the word a mass or lump, but in such scarcity the living was scanty; and since the king had his own bakers, bread fetched from a common place was coarse and no doubt black. Yet he makes the meanness a mercy. At home the prophet might have been stoned by a famished people, or robbed of everything; in prison he was safe and fed when he could not have got bread by labour or begging or money. God brought aid only in a measure, not being pleased to deliver him wholly, yet did not let him be reduced to extremities.
